content.comment_body: Good evening, as the topic suggests, how many slave modules can a [product_name] master communicate with? Is it possible to set up a master device with 44 I/O (24 inputs and 20 outputs), and have 4 slave modules each with 44 I/O (24 inputs and 20 outputs)? Thanks.

Yes, you can configure this, but it's not ideal. You can connect up to 9 [product_name] units, all as masters. This way, each device runs its own program, giving you more capacity—8 x 400 blocks in total. If you use a single master and up to 8 slaves, only one program is available, and typically 400 blocks can't handle so many inputs and outputs. Refer to the operating instructions, chapter 2, for details. Regards, [user_name]

I also suggest using masters rather than slaves, since a slave can only handle 32 bits (inputs plus outputs). So, the configuration of 24 inputs and 20 outputs you plan is not feasible. Overall, a [product_name] device supports a maximum of 64 inputs and 64 outputs. With 4 slaves, you might exceed these input or output limits.
Thanks for clarifying. I’ll use more masters instead. I need 4 [product_name] units which will be sufficient for the 64 inputs and 64 outputs needed.

analysis.insight_summary: Users are discussing the limits and configuration options for connecting multiple slave modules to a [product_name] master. There is some confusion regarding how much I/O can be managed through slave connections, as well as program capacity constraints when using a centralized approach. The discussion highlights that a master-slave configuration can significantly restrict usable I/O and reduce program flexibility, leading users to prefer multiple master units for enhanced functionality.
analysis.user_expectations: The user hopes to link a [product_name] master with several slave modules while maintaining a high number of I/O for each and centralizing control. They expect clear advice regarding system limitations and configuration options.
